name: Reporting File Information (Case 1)
description: Construct a program that receives the full path to an input file from the user, reads that file and reports the number of lines, the longest line, the number of words on each line, and the length of the longest word on each line. Make sure that the program handles each specific exception that could occur.
code:
#Step 1: Define the function
def get_stat(file_name):
    #Step 1.1: Assign initial value to variable that we need for reporting the file information
    num_lines = 0
    longest_line = ""
    #Step 1.2: Enclose the code that might throw an exception within the try block
    try :
        #Step 1.2.1: Open the file and process each line in the file
        myfile = open( file_name, "r")
        for line in myfile:
            num_lines += 1
            num_words = len(line.split())
            #Determine if the line is the longest line so far
            if (len(line) > len(longest_line)) :
                longest_line = line
            #Find the length of the longest word in the line
            longest_word = 0
            for w in line.split() :
                if len(w) > longest_word :
                    longest_word = len(w)
            #Print the line information
            print("Line " + str(num_lines) + " has " + str(num_words) + " tokens (longest = " + str(longest_word) + ")")
        print("Longest line:" + longest_line)
        #Step 1.2.2: Close the file
        myfile.close()
    #Step 1.3: Handle all possible exceptions that may be thrown in the try block 
    except FileNotFoundError:
        print("File not found.")
    except IOError:
        print("Problem with the file!")
#Step 2: Call the function
name = input("Enter the full path of a file: " )
get_stat( name )

commentList: You initialize a counter with num_lines = 0 so you have a starting value that tracks how many lines you have processed; starting at 0 means no lines have been seen yet.
This is a simple assignment statement: the name num_lines is bound to the integer literal 0. Later in the loop the code uses num_lines += 1 to increment this integer each time you read a line.

Be careful not to put this assignment inside the for loop — if you do, you will reset the counter on every iteration and the final count will be wrong. Also avoid initializing it as a string (e.g., '0') because num_lines += 1 would raise a TypeError.

If you forget to initialize num_lines before using it you can get a NameError/UnboundLocalError when you try to increment or read it; initializing it here ensures the variable is local to the function and starts fresh on each call.

As a best practice, use a clear name (like num_lines) and initialize the counter before you enter the try/loop. Note: for simple line numbering you could also use enumerate(file, 1) to avoid manual increments, but this explicit counter is clear and memory-efficient for streaming large files.

commentList: You are creating and initializing the variable that will hold the longest line seen so far; setting longest_line = "" gives you a known starting value to compare against as you read the file.

This is a simple assignment: longest_line = "" sets longest_line to the empty string. Its length is 0, so the first real line you read (with length > 0) will replace it when you do the len(line) > len(longest_line) check.

Avoid setting this to a non-string like 0 or None, because you would then get errors when you call len(longest_line) (len(0) is invalid and len(None) is invalid). Using an empty string avoids special-case checks before using len().

Be aware that lines read from a file usually include the trailing newline character. len(line) therefore counts that newline, which can change which line appears longest. Best practices: keep the name descriptive (longest_line is fine), consider storing a stripped version if you plan to print it cleanly, and handle the empty-file case explicitly (num_lines == 0) so you don't print an empty 'Longest line:' message. commentList: Purpose: You start a try block here so that any errors that occur while opening or reading the file are caught and reported instead of crashing the program; this lets the later except clauses produce user-friendly messages.

Syntax and semantics: In Python 'try' followed by a colon begins an indented suite of statements that will be monitored for exceptions; note that 'try :' is syntactically valid but PEP8 style prefers 'try:'.

Behavior note: If any exception is raised inside this indented block, execution will immediately jump to the first matching except clause below; if no exception occurs the code continues past the except blocks.

Common misconceptions / pitfalls: Don't assume the try alone handles errors — you must have except/finally/else clauses (otherwise you get a SyntaxError). Also avoid wrapping too much code in one try block because you can hide unrelated bugs or make it hard to know what failed.

Best practices: Instead of relying only on try/except for resource cleanup, you should use a context manager (with open(file_name, 'r') as myfile:) so the file is always closed, and you should keep the try block small and catch specific exceptions rather than broad ones to avoid masking other problems.

Exception ordering detail: You handle FileNotFoundError and IOError later; be aware in Python 3 IOError is effectively an alias of OSError and FileNotFoundError is a subclass, so ordering and specificity of except clauses matters when you design your error handling.

commentList: This line opens the named file for reading and assigns the file object to the variable myfile so you can iterate over its lines and perform the counting and longest-word checks that follow.

Breakdown: open(file_name, "r") calls Python's open function with the path (file_name) and mode "r" (read text). open returns a file object that supports iteration and reading; the assignment myfile = ... stores that object for later use.

Possible errors: if the path does not exist you'll get FileNotFoundError; if you lack permission you'll get PermissionError (a kind of IOError); if the file contains bytes that can't be decoded you might see UnicodeDecodeError; if file_name is not a string you could get TypeError.
Common misconceptions: mode "r" is read-only and will not create a file. When you iterate over myfile each line includes its trailing newline, so len(line) counts that newline unless you strip it.

Best practices: open files with a with statement (for example, with open(file_name, "r", encoding="utf-8") as myfile:) so the file is closed automatically. Consider specifying encoding and error handling to avoid decode errors.
Practical tip: validate or normalize the user-provided path (for example with os.path) before opening if you need to handle platform differences or common input mistakes.

commentList: You start a loop that reads the file one line at a time: 'for line in myfile:' runs the indented block once for every line so you can process each line to count lines, words, and find the longest line/word.

You should know the syntax: on each iteration Python takes the next line from the file object and assigns it to the variable 'line'; the colon and the following indented block form the loop body that executes for each line.
You get lines lazily — by iterating the file object directly you read one line at a time instead of loading the whole file into memory, so you won't run out of memory on large files.

Be aware that the string in 'line' usually includes the trailing newline character, so if you use len(line) you are also counting that newline; if you want to ignore trailing whitespace you can use len(line.rstrip()) before comparing lengths.

Watch out for blank lines and token counting: you might expect a blank line to give one token, but line.split() returns an empty list for a line with only whitespace, so you should expect num_words to be 0 for blank lines.

Best practice: rather than manually opening and later calling myfile.close(), you should use 'with open(file_name, 'r') as myfile:' so the file is closed automatically if an error occurs; you can also use enumerate(myfile, 1) to get the line number instead of manually incrementing num_lines.

commentList: You store in num_words the number of tokens found on the current line so you can report how many words that line contains.

You call line.split() with no arguments: this splits the string on any whitespace (spaces, tabs, newlines) and collapses consecutive whitespace into single separators; len(...) then returns how many tokens resulted.
If the line is empty or contains only whitespace, line.split() returns an empty list and len(...) gives 0, which correctly reports zero words for that line.

Don't assume tokens == clean words: punctuation sticks to tokens (for example 'hello,' is one token). If you need words without punctuation you should strip punctuation or use a tokenizer before counting.

Be careful not to use split(' ') if you want robust word counts: split(' ') treats consecutive spaces differently and can produce empty strings, whereas split() with no argument handles arbitrary whitespace more reliably.

A small optimization / best practice: you call line.split() again later (line 18). Instead of calling split() twice, assign tokens = line.split() once and reuse tokens here and in the later loop to avoid repeated work.

This line normally won't raise an exception because line comes from iterating the file (a string). If line could be None or not a string, len() or split() would raise a TypeError, so make sure you iterate real file lines.

commentList: Purpose: This line checks whether the current line from the file is longer than the longest line you have seen so far. If the condition is true, the program will update the stored longest line so you end up with the overall longest line after reading the whole file.

Syntax and semantics: if starts a conditional. len(line) returns the number of characters in the current line and len(longest_line) returns the number in the stored longest line; the > operator compares those numbers. The colon (:) is required to start the indented block that runs when the condition is true. Parentheses around the condition are optional in Python.

Common misconceptions and pitfalls: len(line) includes the newline character and any leading or trailing spaces, so a line with a trailing '\n' or extra spaces may appear longer than you expect. Also, because you use > (greater-than), you keep the first line seen when two lines have the same length; if you wanted the later one you would use >= instead.

Errors to watch for: forgetting the colon causes a SyntaxError, and wrong indentation of the following line will change program behavior or cause an IndentationError. Comparing against longest_line works because it was initialized to an empty string; if you changed that initial value you could get wrong results.

Best practices: if you want to ignore the trailing newline or outer spaces when deciding length, compare len(line.rstrip('\n')) or len(line.strip()). Consider storing longest_line = line.rstrip('\n') so printing is cleaner. Also prefer using a with open(file_name, 'r') as myfile pattern elsewhere to ensure files are closed even on errors.

commentList: Purpose: this line updates the program's record of the longest line so far — when the current line is longer than the previous longest, you assign that current line to longest_line so you can report it later.

Syntax and semantics: this is a simple assignment. The name longest_line now refers to the string value of line. Because Python strings are immutable, you are binding a new string object to longest_line rather than modifying an existing string.

Control-flow detail: this line runs only if the preceding if condition is true (len(line) > len(longest_line)). Because the code uses > and not >=, if two lines have equal length you keep the first one encountered; use >= if you prefer the later one to win.

Whitespace/newline caveat: len(line) includes the trailing newline and any spaces, so your decision may be affected by those characters. If you want to ignore the newline when comparing or storing, use a stripped version like line.rstrip('\n') or line.strip() before comparing and assigning.

Common misconceptions and errors: a learner might think this changes the prior string in place — it does not. Another common mistake is wrong indentation: if this assignment is not indented under the if, it will run unconditionally and break the logic.

Best practices: consider storing a cleaned version (e.g., line.rstrip('\n')) so the printed 'Longest line' doesn't include a trailing newline. Also consider opening files with a with statement (context manager) so resources are closed automatically — that keeps code safer even though closing is handled elsewhere here.

Edge cases: if the file is empty longest_line stays an empty string (''), which is valid but means you'll print nothing after the 'Longest line:' label unless you handle that case explicitly. If lines can be extremely large and you only need the length, you could store lengths instead of whole lines to save memory.

Potential errors and misconceptions: if longest_word were initialized as a string (e.g., "") you would get a TypeError when comparing int and str. 22.content: print("Line " + str(num_lines) + " has " + str(num_words) + " tokens (longest = " + str(longest_word) + ")")
commentList: You use this line to print the per-line report: it shows the line number, the number of tokens (words) on that line, and the length of the longest word on that line in the exact format "Line X has Y tokens (longest = Z)".

You are calling the print() function and building one long string by concatenating pieces with +. The numeric values (num_lines, num_words, longest_word) are converted to strings with str() so they can be joined with the other text.

Be careful: if you forget to convert a number with str(), you will get a TypeError because you cannot concatenate an int to a string. Also note that num_words comes from line.split(), so your word count collapses multiple spaces and will include punctuation as part of words. Finally, longest_line elsewhere still contains the line's trailing newline character, which can make output look like it has extra blank lines.

For clearer and safer code, you should prefer an f-string or comma-separated print for readability, for example: print(f"Line {num_lines} has {num_words} tokens (longest = {longest_word})"). Also consider stripping the line (line = line.rstrip()) before measuring or printing to avoid counting or printing trailing newlines, and use a with open(...) block to handle files so you don't need to call close().

You should also consider using a with-statement to open the file (with open(file_name, 'r') as myfile:) so the file is closed automatically even if an exception occurs; that keeps this print reliable and your code safer.

commentList: This calls the file object's close() method to tell Python you are done with the file so the operating system can free the resource (file handle) that was used to read it.
Syntactically, myfile.close() is a method call: myfile is the file object and the parentheses () mean you are invoking the close method; close() itself returns None.
If open(file_name, "r") failed and myfile was never created, calling myfile.close() would raise a NameError — so you must ensure the file object exists before you try to close it.

Because this close() is inside the try block, an exception raised before this line will skip the close and leave the file open; to make sure the file is always closed even on errors, you should use a finally block or a context manager.

Best practice: prefer using a context manager (with open(file_name, "r") as myfile:) so Python automatically closes the file for you; if you do call close() manually, check that myfile is defined and not already closed.

After you call close(), the myfile variable still exists but the file is closed — any further reads or writes will raise an error, so make sure you only close when you are truly finished with the file.

commentList: You use this line to start an except block that runs when the try block raises a FileNotFoundError — typically when the file path you supplied does not exist.
You must write it exactly as shown: 'except FileNotFoundError:' followed by an indented block. The colon and indentation tell Python which statements belong to this exception handler.

You should not assume this catches every file problem. FileNotFoundError only covers a missing file; other problems (permission errors, decoding errors, etc.) may raise different exceptions and need their own handlers.

Be careful with ordering: you put this more specific exception before broader ones (like IOError). If you reversed the order, the broader handler could catch the error first and this line would never run.

For better feedback and debugging, consider capturing the exception object (except FileNotFoundError as e:) and include the file name or error message in your print. Also prefer using 'with open(...)' so you don't have to manually close the file.

commentList: Purpose: This line handles the specific error that occurs when the program tries to open a file that does not exist. If you give a wrong path or a file name that isn't present, this block runs so the program doesn't crash and instead prints a helpful message.

Syntax and semantics: 'except FileNotFoundError:' is Python's way to say "if a FileNotFoundError was raised in the try block, run the indented code that follows." The colon starts the except block, and the following indented print runs only when that exact error happens. You can also write 'except FileNotFoundError as e:' if you want to inspect the error object.

Common misconceptions and pitfalls: Don't assume this catches every file-related problem — it only catches the "file not found" case. Permission errors or other I/O problems may raise different exceptions (for example PermissionError or other OSError variants). Also be aware of resource leaks: if the file was already opened earlier and a different error happens later, you might still need to ensure the file is closed (use 'with open(...)' or a finally block).

Best practices: Instead of a generic message, you should give the user more context (for example include the file name), or show the system message by capturing the exception: 'except FileNotFoundError as e: print("File not found:", file_name, e)'. Also prefer 'with open(...)' to open the file so you don't have to worry about closing it if an exception occurs.

commentList: This line starts an exception handler that runs if an I/O error occurs while you are working with the file (for example, a read or write problem). It lets the program report a user-friendly message instead of crashing.

In syntax terms, 'except IOError:' catches exceptions whose type is IOError or any subclass. The code block that follows this line will execute only when such an exception is raised in the preceding try block.

Because you already have 'except FileNotFoundError:' above, that specific error will be handled first. Order matters: you put more specific exceptions before more general ones so the right handler runs.

Be careful with a common misconception: in Python 3, IOError is essentially an alias of OSError, and many file-related errors (like PermissionError or FileNotFoundError) are subclasses of OSError. If you rely on IOError, know how it maps to other exception types in your Python version.

A practical improvement is to capture the exception object so you can see details (for example: 'except IOError as e:') and either log e or include it in a diagnostic message. That helps you debug problems instead of only showing a vague message.

Also note that closing the file is done inside the try block. If an exception is raised before myfile.close(), the file may remain open. A better practice is to use a context manager ('with open(file_name, "r") as myfile:') or a finally block to ensure the file is always closed.

Avoid catching overly broad error types unless you handle them properly. You should prefer catching specific exceptions you expect (e.g., PermissionError) and provide clear guidance to the user about what to do next.

32.content: name = input("Enter the full path of a file: " )
commentList: Purpose: This line asks you (at the console) to type the full path of the file to analyze and saves whatever you type into the variable name so the program can pass it to get_stat(name).

Syntax and semantics: input("Enter the full path of a file: ") prints the prompt and returns the text you enter as a string; the = operator assigns that string to the variable name. This is the Python 3 form of input (in Python 2 you would use raw_input).

Possible errors and misconceptions: input can raise EOFError or KeyboardInterrupt if there is no input available or the user cancels; the returned string might be empty if you just press Enter; input does not check whether the file exists or is readable (that check happens later, producing FileNotFoundError or IOError). Also note that backslashes you type on Windows are handled as characters by input (no escaping is needed here), but stray leading/trailing spaces will be kept unless you remove them.

Best practices: strip whitespace right away (for example, name = input(...).strip()) so you don't get accidental leading/trailing spaces; expand user paths and normalize them (os.path.expanduser, os.path.abspath or use pathlib.Path) before opening; use a clear variable name like file_name to match the function parameter; and consider wrapping the input and subsequent call in try/except to handle EOFError/KeyboardInterrupt gracefully and give the user a helpful message.

Syntax & semantics: get_stat(name) is a function call — the name of the function followed by parentheses containing the argument variable name. The current value stored in name is passed into the function when you run this line.
Where the argument comes from: name was set by the previous input(...) call, so you are passing the string the user typed (the file path) into get_stat.

No capture of return value: you do not assign the call to a variable because get_stat prints its results directly. If you wanted to use the results in code, you would change get_stat to return data and then assign it here (for example: stats = get_stat(name)).

Common mistakes to avoid: if you forget the parentheses and write get_stat, you only reference the function object and do not execute it. If you call get_stat with the wrong number of arguments (for example get_stat() when the function requires one), Python raises a TypeError.

Potential runtime issues: if name is an empty string or points to a non-existent path, get_stat will handle FileNotFoundError and IOError inside the function and print an error message. However, other unexpected errors could still propagate, so be aware of that.

distractors.description: Step-by-step why you might pick this: when you see a line as text you may assume iterating over it gives you words, so using the line directly feels simpler and avoids extra calls. This looks short and familiar if you have iterated strings before. What happens if you use this line instead: the loop will iterate over each character in the line (including spaces and the newline), not over words. As a result, when the program computes the length of each loop item you will almost always get 1 (single characters) or possibly 0 for some special cases, so the reported "longest word" on the line will be wrong (typically 1) even though the reported token count uses a correct splitting earlier. There is no runtime error, but the output will be incorrect. Why this is invalid here: you need to examine actual words (sequences of non-space characters), not characters. This distractor misses the required tokenization step and so produces incorrect longest-word lengths.

You might pick this because it looks shorter and you may (mistakenly) expect Python to compare the word's length to the stored longest-word value automatically. In reality, w is a string and longest_word is an integer, so using '>' between them will cause a type error at runtime: Python cannot compare str and int with '>'. That means the program will crash the first time it reaches this line instead of correctly finding the longest word length. The mistake here is a types mix-up: you used the word itself where you needed its length (or you should have used a numeric value on both sides). This distractor is plausible because beginners sometimes think Python will coerce types for you or that comparing strings and numbers is allowed, but it is invalid because the types are incompatible.

You might pick this if you intend to store the longest word itself rather than its character count, confusing the variable's role as a numeric maximum length with a string holder. What happens if you use this line: on the next iteration, when the code evaluates `if len(w) > longest_word :`, Python will attempt to compare an integer `len(w)` with a string `longest_word`, resulting in a `TypeError: '>' not supported between instances of 'int' and 'str'`. Why this is invalid here: the variable `longest_word` is initialized to integer `0` and is used to store the numeric length (as displayed in the formatted output `longest = ...`), not the word object itself.
